Connections puzzles: test the link against every clue

The first association is only a candidate. A good connection has to explain the whole set.

In this article
  1. Your first thought can be useful—and incomplete
  2. Make the category specific enough to check
  3. Pay attention to the awkward clue
  4. After the reveal, explain the weakest fit
Related gameConnections →

Your first thought can be useful—and incomplete

Read these four words: bark, trunk, leaf, root. ‘Tree’ is an immediate connection. But bark can also be a dog’s sound, a trunk can hold luggage, and a root can belong to an equation.

A connection puzzle makes you choose which meaning matters in this particular set. Start with your first association, then test it. A strong answer should explain all the clues through the same idea.

Make the category specific enough to check

‘Things you can find outside’ is broad enough to accept almost anything. ‘Parts of a tree’ makes a sharper claim. You can examine each word and ask whether it belongs.

In BrainiLab Connections, you choose the relationship from the available answers. Do not assume it uses the rules of another game with a similar name. Read the prompt and choices before deciding what counts as a successful answer.

Try mentally completing the sentence ‘Each clue is a…’ or ‘Each word can follow…’. If you have to change the sentence for one clue, your connection may be too loose.

Pay attention to the awkward clue

Suppose three clues fit your idea immediately and one refuses. Instead of treating the awkward word as an exception, make it the centre of your next attempt. List another meaning for that word and see whether it changes your reading of the other three.

This is a practical pause, not a demand to invent dozens of possibilities. Test a small number of precise alternatives. The goal is to find a common explanation, not the most imaginative story.

What links keys, space and return in a familiar computer context?

A keyboard. “Space” and “return” can name keys, while “keys” gives the broader context. The context matters: those words have other meanings too.

After the reveal, explain the weakest fit

When the answer appears, choose the clue you understood least well and explain how it fits. If it uses an unfamiliar meaning, look that meaning up rather than simply memorising the answer label.

For your next round, remember the move that helped: checking a second meaning, tightening the category or testing the odd clue. That is something you can reuse even when none of the words repeat.
